opening_message:
Ticket 1: Casey Wu (employee ID E005) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E005.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Casey Wu (E005) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting write access to Source Code. As a full-time employee, write is permitted (admin would require owning the system, which is not the case here). Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E005 (Casey Wu) is a contractor with basic security training (note: this conflicts with the HR note saying full-time). Contractors max at read without advanced training. Requested write exceeds the maximum, so recommend granting read.
reason: The request is for write access to Source Code. The HR note states Casey Wu is full-time (max write), while the Security note states the Security DB shows contractor with basic security training (max read without advanced training). These records conflict on employment type. Given the conflicting data, I resolve conservatively in favor of the lower access level consistent with the Security record and recommendation. As a contractor with basic training, the maximum permitted is read; the requested write exceeds that, so grant read.

Ticket 1: Casey Wu (E005) requests write access to Source Code.

- HR agent: role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommends write
- Security agent: role Payroll Specialist, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read

The HR agent looked up employment type in own database: full_time.
The Security agent looked up employment type in own database: contractor.

The Security agent also did not look up role (same value as HR).

1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If contractor with basic training: max read, requested write → grant read.

Hmm, let me weigh: HR agent looked up employment type in own database: full_time. Security agent looked up employment type in own database: contractor. Both have primary sources.

Without additional information, I think the approver should resolve conflicts conservatively: grant read (the maximum under contractor interpretation, also the security recommendation). Granting write would be safe only if full-time is correct. Given uncertainty, least privilege suggests read.

Actually, let me reconsider the nature of these tasks. This appears to be a multi-agent simulation where the approver must decide. The correct approach might be to notice the conflict and choose the lower access level as the safe option, since we can't verify. The Security team's data is often authoritative for access.

Actually wait - policy: "Never grant more than the requested level" - requested write. If we treat as full-time, max write → grant write. If contractor, max read → grant read.
